paper.page: Grant: A Framework for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with Multi-Attribute Range Filters Daichi Amagata The University of Osaka amagata.daichi@ist.osaka-u.ac.jp Abstract Recently, academia and industry have considered the problem of approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) with filters. In this setting, each object consists of a high-dimensional vector and attribute values. Given a query vector, filters for attribute values, and 𝑘, this problem retrieves 𝑘 vectors approximately nearest to the query vector among a set of objects passing the filters. This paper considers range filters, i.e., users can specify a range constraint for each attribute. Most existing works do not consider this setting, and they assume (i) only a single attribute or (ii) matching filters that require the same attribute values or categories. Existing techniques for these assumptions are not available for our setting or are trivially not efficient. Although standard solutions, such as pre-filter and post-filter, can handle our problem, they are also inefficient. Some works tackle the same problem as ours, but their techniques necessitate historical query workloads, which significantly limit practical use cases. To remove these limitations, this work proposes Grant, a novel framework that solves this problem efficiently while accepting arbitrary range filters and ANNS data structures. Grant can guarantee a search time sub-linear to the number of objects, which is not held by existing techniques. We conduct extensive experiments, and their results demonstrate that Grant outperforms existing techniques. 1 Introduction Modern search engines increasingly rely on machine learning models that embed many types of objects, such as images and texts, into high-dimensional vectors. Due to this fact, the problem of similarity search in a high-dimensional space becomes more important in many fields, such as recommender systems [1, 2], information retrieval [6, 5, 8, 24, 23], databases [35, 44, 54, 45], artificial intelligence [27], and machine learning [3, 4]. For example, computing the exact nearest neighbor on large data with high dimensionality is computationally expensive, and many applications, such as RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), allow approximate results [28]. Therefore, approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) has been studied extensively [7]. Nowadays, to enable making use of attribute information associated with objects, ANNS with attribute filters has been considered both in academia [51, 20, 48, 58, 53, 37] and industry (e.g., Alibaba [50], Apple [34], and Microsoft [57, 19]). As specified in these industrial works, the problem of ANNS with attribute filters is also important in many real-world Web applications. A typical example of this problem is that, in e-commerce scenarios, each user finds the products most similar to a given query vector among a set of objects satisfying attribute filters (e.g., price, rating, and production date). Similarly, RAG applications receive benefits from ANNS with attribute filters. For example, when a user wants to know health risk, he/she may write a prompt like “investigate what symptoms tend to appear for people aged from 40 to 50 and with blood pressure at least 140.” This script is transformed into an ANNS with range filters on age and blood pressure attributes, and the large language model obtains the answer from the retriever. 1.1 Limitations of Prior Work The existing works on the problem of ANNS with attribute filters have the following issues. (1) Single attribute assumption. Many existing works [51, 58, 53, 37, 30, 52, 49, 55] assume that each object has only a single attribute, and their techniques are available only in this case. (Although some works [53, 58, 15, 30, 55] consider range filters, they cannot deal with multiple attributes, or they are reduced to the standard technique, Post-filter, which is introduced in Section 2.) This setting significantly limits applications, and objects generally have multiple attributes, as seen in the above examples. (2) Dealing with only matching filters. Most existing works consider attribute “matching” as a filter [26, 51, 20, 19, 48, 37, 13], i.e., a filter evaluates whether a given object has the same attribute value/category as that of this filter. As the above 1 arXiv:2610.11563v1 [cs.DB] 8 Oct 2026

application examples show, users typically specify “range” filters, e.g., they want items whose prices and production dates fall within certain ranges. Obviously, existing techniques for matching filters are inefficient for range filters on multiple attributes, as they require running for each filter in multiple continuous ranges, which necessitates an infinite number of iterations. (3) Always requiring past queries. Although some works [34, 29] consider range filters on multiple attributes, they necessitate past queries. They build ANNS indices based on past queries, so they do not function without past queries. This strong assumption significantly limits practical use cases. A better and practical property is that an ANNS algorithm works well without past query workloads and its efficiency can be accelerated with past queries. Note that no work devised optimal algorithms for ANNS with range filters on multiple attributes, without past query workloads. (4) Vector data management systems are general but inefficient. Some vector data management systems, e.g., [50, 46, 41], support multiple attributes and range filters. They, however, do not optimize ANNS algorithms for this setting, and their approaches are essentially Pre-filter or Post-filter. 1.2 Contribution This paper tackles the problem of ANNS with multi-attribute range filters, a more general and challenging problem than those with a single attribute and matching filters. An efficient and generally available solution (i) must be a workload-free structure and (ii) has an option of past query usage for efficiency acceleration. No existing works satisfy efficiency and generality at the same time for this problem. This paper proposes Grant (Graph in tree index), an efficient framework for this problem, and it incorporates graph indices into a tree index. It has three main advantages: (i) It handles multiple attributes and arbitrary ranges, optimized for practical scenarios. (ii) It can employ arbitrary state-of-the-art multi-dimensional tree index and proximity graph. (iii) It functions well without any past query workloads, and its efficiency can be enhanced with past query vectors. (iv) It is fast and accurate in practice. To summarize, our main contributions are as follows. • We propose Grant, a new and general framework for the problem of ANNS with multi-attribute range filters, and it is built without any past query workloads. • We present an efficient range-filtered ANNS algorithm that exploits the Grant structure. If past query vectors are avail- able, the efficiency of the proposed algorithm can be accelerated. • When we use a kd-tree [12] as a base structure of Grant, Grant can have a theoretical guarantee that the ANNS time is sub-linear to 𝑛, where 𝑛 is the number of objects. This theoretical result is not achieved by existing algorithms for ANNS with range filters on multiple attributes. • We conduct extensive experiments, and their results demonstrate that Grant outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in most tests. 2 Preliminary 2.1 Problem Definition Let 𝑋 be a set of 𝑛 objects. Each object 𝑥 𝑖 ∈ 𝑋 has a 𝑑-dimensional vector 𝐯 𝑖 and 𝑚 attribute values 𝐚 𝑖 , i.e., 𝑥 𝑖 = (𝐯 𝑖 , 𝐚 𝑖 ) where 𝑑 is large and 𝑚 ≥ 2. Notice that the 𝑚 attribute values can be represented as an 𝑚-dimensional vector, so we use 𝑎 𝑖 [𝑗] to denote the 𝑗-th attribute value of 𝐚 𝑖 . Let 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(⋅, ⋅) be the distance between two vectors. The problem of 𝑘 nearest neighbor search with multi-attribute range filters is defined as follows: Definition 1 (𝑘 nearest neighbor search with multi-attribute range filters). Given an object set 𝑋, a query vector 𝐪, query range filters 𝐹 = {[𝑙 1 , 𝑢 1 ], ..., [𝑙 𝑚 , 𝑢 𝑚 ]}, and a result size 𝑘, this problem retrieves a set 𝑆 ∗ (𝐪, 𝐹 ) of 𝑘 objects such that (i) 𝑆 ∗ (𝐪, 𝐹 ) ⊆ 𝑋(𝐹 ) and (ii) ∀𝑥 ∈ 𝑆 ∗ (𝐪, 𝐹 ) and ∀𝑥 ′ ∈ 𝑋(𝐹 )\𝑆 ∗ (𝐪, 𝐹 ), 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐯, 𝐪) ≤ 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐯 ′ , 𝐪), where 𝑋(𝐹 ) = {𝑥 | 𝑥 ∈ 𝑋, ∀𝑗 ∈ [1, 𝑚], 𝑙 𝑗 ≤ 𝑎[𝑗] ≤ 𝑢 𝑗 }. Ties are broken arbitrarily. If |𝑋(𝐹 )| < 𝑘, we return 𝑋(𝐹 ). This paper considers an approximation version of the above problem. We search for 𝑆(𝐪, 𝐹 ) such that 𝑆(𝐪, 𝐹 ) ⊆ 𝑋(𝐹 ), |𝑆(𝐪, 𝐹 )| = 𝑘, but we may have 𝑆(𝐪, 𝐹 ) ≠ 𝑆 ∗ (𝐪, 𝐹 ). To measure the accuracy of 𝑆, we use recall@𝑘, a criterion commonly used in ANNS studies, and 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙@𝑘 = |𝑆(𝐪, 𝐹 ) ∩ 𝑆 ∗ (𝐪, 𝐹 )| 𝑘 . 2

ANNS with Matching Filter. Many works consider this setting [51, 19, 48, 37, 13, 42]. For example, FilteredVamana [19] extends Vamana by adding a label for each edge. During ANNS, only edges with the label matching a given filter are traversed. StitchedVamana is another variant of Vamana, and it is a Vamana of the objects having the same label (or attribute value). That is, for each distinct label, a StitchedVamana is built. NHQ [48] defines a customized distance function that considers vector and label similarities. A proximity graph is built based on this customized distance function. They do not support multi-attribute cases and/or range filters. ANNS with Range Filter. Recent studies [58, 53] considered how to support a range filter in HNSW. SeRF [58] requires 𝑂(𝑛 2 ) space, and iRangeGraph reduced this space to 𝑂(𝑛 log 𝑛). Another work [15] developed a different data structure based on a segment tree, and it also needs 𝑂(𝑛 log 𝑛) space. Literature [30] further reduces the space complexity to 𝑂(𝑛). These works focus on a single attribute case, and [53] suggests that their approaches are reduced to Post-filter when query filters specify multiple attributes. WoW [49] achieves an updatable index for ANNS with a single range filter. HQI [34] and SIEVE [29] can deal with multi-attribute range filters, but they require historical query filters to build the structures. That is, without this assumption, their structures cannot be built. (Without past filters, SIEVE is reduced to a standard algorithm, e.g., Post-filter on a graph index.) Furthermore, HQI focuses on batch query processing, and this setting is different from our objective, i.e., processing each ANN query efficiently while providing a high recall result. Unlike these works, the Grant structure can be built without any past information. Vector Data Management Systems. Milvus [46], NaviX [41], and ADBV [50] support multi-attribute range filters. Milvus can select an ANNS index, e.g., graph index and IVF (inverted file index), whereas ADBV employs IVF. ADBV proposes two approaches: one is Pre-filter, and the other is the verification of a subset of 𝑋. Specifically, when IVF is used, only some posting lists similar to a given query vector are verified. This verification is the same as the brute-force algorithm introduced in Section 2. NaviX also employs Pre-filter but runs an approximate verification. Milvus also employs Pre-filter and considers Post-filter. 4 Grant Main idea. Indexing low-dimensional data is a classic problem, and many famous tree-based indices, such as kd-tree [12] and R-tree [21], are known. These data structures support efficient orthogonal (or axis-parallel) range queries. Because the attribute values held by the objects in 𝑋 are regarded as low-dimensional vectors, we can build a tree index based on the attribute values. Then, for example, 𝑋(𝐹 ) can be efficiently obtained with a range query of 𝐹 . This approach avoids accessing many vectors that do not satisfy 𝐹 . However, simply applying this idea results in Pre-filter, so we suffer from a high computational cost when |𝑋(𝐹 )| is large. (If 𝑛 is large, e.g., tens of millions, |𝑋(𝐹 )| = 0.01 ⋅ 𝑛 is still large.) On the other hand, assume that 𝑋 is indexed by a graph index (i.e., based on the 𝑑-dimensional vectors). Although this approach yields a fast search time for ANNS without filters, our approach is limited to Post-filter when filters are specified. Post-filter may need to access many objects (vectors) that do not satisfy 𝐹 . Now we have a challenging question: Given a query vector 𝐪 and query filters 𝐹 , how can we access only objects that satisfy 𝐹 and are similar to 𝐪? The above observations of the tree and graph indices actually suggest an idea yielding a positive answer to this question. If we receive benefits of the tree and graph indices (if we can run graph-based ANNS on the range query result of 𝐹 ), we overcome the above challenge. We propose Grant, which achieves this idea. 4.1 Grant Structure Existing indices do not have the ability to navigate objects that pass a given filter and have vectors similar to 𝐪. The novelty of Grant is this navigation ability. Grant is a tree structure in which leaf nodes have a capacity of 𝑂(𝑛/𝑐), where 𝑐 is a constant and hyper-parameter. This tree structure is constructed based on the attribute values. Each object in 𝑋 is maintained by a leaf node of the Grant, and each leaf node maintains the 𝑂(𝑛/𝑐) objects by using a graph index  based on their 𝑑-dimensional vectors. Note that the number of leaf nodes in Grant is 𝑂(𝑐) = 𝑂(1). Figure 1 illustrates an example of the Grant structure, assuming that each node can have at most two child nodes. This combination of tree and graph structures is simple yet effective: The main merits of this structure are as follows. (i) A set of objects having similar attribute values can be maintained by a graph index, i.e., attribute-based and vector-based navigation is simultaneously achieved. (ii) No past information is required. These properties are not held by existing techniques for our problem and are important to positively answer the challenging question mentioned earlier and yield a fast ANNS time described in Theorem 1. Grant construction. This construction is done only once, and the Grant is general to any query vectors and range filters. Let  be the base tree structure of Grant. We use a top-down tree-building approach, and the Grant is built based on the construction algorithm of  . We assume that it is a balanced tree. 4

Figure 1: Grant structure. Grey nodes represent leaf nodes, each of which maintains a graph index. Algorithm 1: Build(𝑋, 𝑐) Input: 𝑋, 𝑐 1 root node of  ← Make-Node(𝑋, 𝑐) 2 return  3 Function Make-Node(𝑌 , 𝑐): 4 𝑢 ← a new node of  5 if |𝑌 | ≤ 𝑛/𝑐 then 6 Build-Graph(𝑌 ) 7 return 𝑢 8 𝑌 𝑙 , 𝑌 𝑟 ← Split(𝑌 ) 9 left child node of 𝑢 ← Make-Node(𝑌 𝑙 , 𝑐) 10 right child node of 𝑢 ← Make-Node(𝑌 𝑟 , 𝑐) 11 return 𝑢 Algorithm 1 describes the constuction algorithm. Building  is performed by Make-Node(⋅, 𝑐). Given 𝑋, we make a root node of  . If |𝑋| ≤ 𝑛/𝑐, it is a leaf node, and we build a graph index  based on the 𝑑-dimensional vectors in 𝑋. ( is an arbitrary graph index.) Otherwise, we equally split 𝑋 based on the construction algorithm of  (i.e., based on attribute values) to make  balanced. We then create its descendant nodes in a recursive manner. Proposition 1. Let 𝑓 (𝑛) be the time of splitting a given set of 𝑛 objects. Also, let 𝑔(𝑛) be the time of building a given proximity graph of the object set. A Grant is built in 𝑂(𝑛(1 + 𝑓 (𝑛))) + 𝑔(𝑛) time 1 . Proof. Since  is a balanced tree, the height of  is at most log 𝑐 = 𝑂(1) (recall that each leaf node can manage at most 𝑛/𝑐 objects and 𝑐 = 𝑂(1)). In addition, the number of nodes of  is ≤ 2𝑐 − 1 = 𝑂(𝑐) = 𝑂(1). Hence,  can be built in 𝑂(𝑛(log 𝑐 + 𝑓 (𝑛))) = 𝑂(𝑛(1 + 𝑓 (𝑛))) time. The remaining cost we need to consider is that of building a graph index in each leaf node. When we call Build-Graph(𝑌 ) in Algorithm 1, |𝑌 | ≤ 𝑛/𝑐. Because the number of leaf nodes is at most 𝑐 = 𝑂(1), the total cost of building the graph indices is 𝑔(𝑛). It is now clear that this proposition holds. Proposition 2 (Space complexity of a Grant). Let 𝑆(𝑛) be the space of a given proximity graph, and a Grant needs 𝑂(1) + 𝑆(𝑛) space. Proof. Recall the following three facts. (i) Each object in 𝑋 is maintained in a leaf node of  . (ii)  has 𝑂(𝑐) = 𝑂(1) nodes, because the Grant has 𝑐 = 𝑂(1) leaf nodes. (iii) Each graph has 𝑆(𝑛) space. Given these, this proposition is true. 4.2 ANNS on Grant Algorithm 2 describes our approach to running ANNS with multi-attribute range filters on the Grant. We first run a range query of 𝐹 on the Grant and obtain a set of leaf nodes 𝑈 that overlap with 𝐹 . Then, for each 𝑢 ∈ 𝑈 , we run a graph-based ANNS algorithm and pick only objects satisfying 𝐹 . Note that each leaf node may partially overlap 𝐹 , so some objects maintained in a given leaf node may not satisfy 𝐹 . Figure 2 depicts an example. 1 As seen in Section 5, Grant is built quickly, e.g., within a few minutes on ten million objects. Hence, as long as 𝑋 is not frequently updated, rebuilding Grant is practical for dynamic 𝑋 (e.g., batch updates). 5

Algorithm 2: Query( , 𝐪, 𝐹 , 𝑘) Input:  (Grant), 𝐪, 𝐹 , 𝑘 1 𝑆(𝐪, 𝐹 ) ← ∅ 2 𝑈 ← Range-Search( , 𝐹 ) 3 foreach 𝑢 ∈ 𝑈 do 4 𝑆 ′ ← ANNS(, 𝐪, 𝑘) 5 foreach 𝑥 ∈ 𝑆 ′ such that 𝑥 satisfies 𝐹 do 6 Update 𝑆(𝐪, 𝐹 ) if necessary 7 return 𝑆 One of our main results is that this approach theoretically sounds and is practically fast, as analyzed below. Note that ̃ 𝑂(⋅) hides any polylog factors. Lemma 1. Let 𝑇 (𝑛) be the time of a range search on  of 𝑛 objects. Our algorithm can run in 𝑇 (𝑛) + ̃ 𝑂(1) time. Proof. Line 2 requires 𝑇 (𝑛) time. We rely on the recent result [31], and there exists a proximity graph that deals with ANNS(, 𝐪, 𝑘) in ̃ 𝑂(1) worst time 2 . Since the number leaf nodes is at most 𝑐 = 𝑂(1), |𝑈 | = 𝑂(1). Therefore, lines 3–6 need ̃ 𝑂(1) time. Existing works that can deal with this problem have no time bound, but our algorithm can yield a sub-linear query time. Theorem 1. If we use a kd-tree as the base tree structure of a Grant, our algorithm can run in 𝑂(𝑛 1−1/𝑚 ) time. Proof. A range search on a kd-tree needs 𝑂(𝑛 1−1/𝑚 + OUT) time, where OUT is the result size of the range search [12]. Then, 𝑇 (𝑛) = 𝑂(𝑛 1−1/𝑚 + |𝑈 |) = 𝑂(𝑛 1−1/𝑚 ). Note that 𝑂(𝑛 1−1/𝑚 ) >̃ 𝑂(1). From Lemma 1, this theorem holds. 4.3 Optimizing ANNS on Grant by Heuristic An interesting observation of the above algorithm is that, although Theorem 1 suggests that the main cost of our algorithm is the range search theoretically, the main “practical” cost is derived from the graph-based ANNS of each leaf node in 𝑈 . It is important to notice that at most 𝑘 leaf nodes have the objects ∈ 𝑆 ∗ (𝐪, 𝐹 ), but we may have |𝑈 | > 𝑘. In this case, our algorithm runs graph-based ANNS on at least |𝑈 | − 𝑘 unnecessary leaf nodes. However, it is hard to know which leaf node has the objects ∈ 𝑆 ∗ (𝐪, 𝐹 ) in advance. We therefore propose heuristic approaches that skip leaf nodes in 𝑈 that would not have the objects ∈ 𝑆 ∗ (𝐪, 𝐹 ). Note that these heuristics are applied only when |𝑈 | > 𝑂(𝑘). Probabilistic node verification. The idea of our heuristic is to make use of an overlapping ratio between 𝐹 and each leaf node in 𝑈 . In Figure 2, although 𝑢 8 overlaps 𝐹 , the overlapping space is very slight against the partition of 𝑢 8 and 𝐹 . Hence, it is intuitive that 𝑢 8 would not have the 𝑘NN objects, suggesting that 𝑢 8 is skippable. This idea is specific to the Grant structure. To implement this idea, we define the overlap ratio between 𝐹 and a leaf node 𝑢. Definition 2. Let 𝑉 (𝐹 ) be the volume of the hyper-rectangle defined by the ranges in 𝐹 . Also, let 𝑉 (𝑢) be the volume of the hyper-rectangle of a node 𝑢. The overlap ratio between 𝐹 and 𝑢, 𝑟(𝐹 , 𝑢), is 𝑟(𝐹 , 𝑢) = max ( 𝑉 (𝐹 ∩ 𝑢) 𝑉 (𝐹 ) , 𝑉 (𝐹 ∩ 𝑢) 𝑉 (𝑢) ) , where 𝐹 ∩ 𝑢 is the overlapping space between 𝐹 and 𝑢. Assuming a local uniform distribution of attributes within a leaf node, the number of valid candidates 𝐸[𝑛 𝑣𝑎𝑙𝑖𝑑 ] is esti- mated as 𝐸[𝑛 𝑣𝑎𝑙𝑖𝑑 | 𝑢, 𝐹 ] ∝ 𝑛 𝑐 ⋅ 𝑟(𝐹 , 𝑢). Nodes with higher 𝐸[𝑛 𝑣𝑎𝑙𝑖𝑑 ] can be prioritized to increase the likelihood of retrieving true nearest neighbors. For 𝑢 ∈ 𝑈 , we have 𝑟(𝐹 , 𝑢) ∈ (0, 1], and 𝑟(𝐹 , 𝑢) is obtained in 𝑂(1) time. Because it is not guaranteed that 𝑘 leaf nodes with the largest overlap ratio have the 𝑘NN objects, we employ a probabilistic approach. Specifically, for each leaf node 𝑢 in the range search result, if 𝑟(𝐹 , 𝑢) is larger than a random real value ∈ (0, 1], we run graph-based ANNS in this leaf node. 2 In our experiments, we used HNSW as a practical instantiation of [31] because it empirically follows similar efficiency trends [33, 40] while providing superior scalability and implementation simplicity for real-world deployments [47, 10, 28]. 6

The grey rectangle shows 𝐹 , and it overlaps with 𝑢 5 , 𝑢 6 , 𝑢 7 , and 𝑢 8 , so we run graph-based ANNS on these leaf nodes. 4.4 Workload-aware ANNS If past query vectors are available, we can enhance our proposed approach. Let 𝐩 be the nearest vector to a given query vector 𝐪 among a set of past query vectors 3 . Furthermore, let 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐩, 𝑢 𝑖 ) be the distance between 𝐩 and the nearest neighbor vector in the leaf node 𝑢 𝑖 of the Grant. For ease of explanation, assume that 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐩, 𝑢 1 ) < 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐩, 𝑢 2 ) < ⋯ 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐩, 𝑢 𝑐 ). Assuming that 𝑘 = 2 and 𝐹 overlaps with 10 leaf nodes, 𝑢 1 , 𝑢 2 , ..., and 𝑢 10 , it is intuitively known that running ANNS of 𝐪 in 𝑢 1 and 𝑢 2 is sufficient to obtain the objects ∈ 𝑆 ∗ (𝐪, 𝐹 ). This is because, if 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐩, 𝐪) is small, 𝐩 and 𝐪 share similar ANNS results. This idea also skips ANNS on unnecessary nodes and enables accessing only 𝑂(𝑘) leaf nodes while keeping high recall. Additional pre-processing. Let 𝐏 be a set of past query vectors, and it is maintained based on a graph index  𝐏 . Addi- tionally, for each past query vector 𝐩 ∈ 𝐏, we run ANNS on each leaf node 𝑢 of the Grant. Let 𝑥 be the object obtained for the ANNS, and we record 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐩, 𝐯). We use a matrix  to maintain such a record:  = ⎛ ⎜ ⎜ ⎝ 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐩 1 , 𝐯 𝛼 ) ⋯ 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐩 1 , 𝐯 𝛽 ) ⋮ ⋱ ⋮ 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐩 𝑐 , 𝐯 𝛾 ) ⋯ 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐩 𝑐 , 𝐯 𝜙 ) ⎞ ⎟ ⎟ ⎠ where the 𝑖-th row 𝑗-th column is the ANN result of 𝐩 𝑖 in the leaf node 𝑢 𝑗 . This is done after running building Grant. Note that this additional pre-processing is also done only once. When an HNSW is used as the index of 𝐏 such that |𝐏| ≤ 𝑛, the additional pre-processing time is ̃ 𝑂(|𝐏|𝑛). This is because building an HNSW of 𝐏 needs 𝑂(|𝐏| log |𝐏|) time [33] and obtaining  requires 𝑂(|𝐏|𝑐) = 𝑂(|𝐏|) time. Similarly, its space complexity is 𝑂(|𝐏|𝑛). (To reduce the time and space complexities, we can randomly sample past queries.) Query processing. Algorithm 3 presents our algorithm for ANNS with multi-attribute range filters on Grant with  𝑃 and . Its main difference from Algorithm 2 is to exploit a past query vector that is similar to a given query vector 𝐪. We obtain a set 𝑈 ′ of leaf nodes that overlap 𝐹 . If |𝑈 ′ | is large, we compute 𝐩 𝑖 , which is an ANN vector to 𝐪 in 𝐏, by running graph-based ANN on  𝐏 . Then, we pick only 𝑂(𝑘) leaf nodes in 𝑈 ′ such that 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝐩 𝑖 , ⋅) is the smallest. The subsequent operations are the same as our original query processing algorithm. This is an optional workload-aware optimization that can be applied on top of Grant when past query vectors are available. 3 This is a different assumption from that of [34, 29], since they assume that not past query vectors but past query filters are available. Our assumption is easier to hold: for example, we can use the vectors in 𝑋 as past query vectors. 7

We used four datasets commonly used in ANNS works: Deep [11], SIFT (http://corpus-texmex.irisa. fr/), SPACEV [14], and T2 (https://big-ann-benchmarks.com/neurips21.html). They are large-scale and contain 10 million vectors. Deep is a set of 96-dimensional deep features, and SIFT is a set of 128-dimensional SIFT features. SPACEV is a set of 100-dimensional learned document vectors, and T2I is a set of 200-dimensional vectors learned from the Yandex visual search engine results. We followed the existing filtered ANNS works [34, 50, 46, 29] to provide each object with attribute values, and the attribute values follow a power-law distribution [20], which reflects real-world scenarios [39]. By default, 𝑚 = 2. Queries. For each dataset, we used 100 random query vectors that can be obtained from the same source of the dataset. Given a query vector 𝐪, to generate query range filters 𝐹 , we first assigned a random value, which also follows the same power-law distribution of the attribute domain, to 𝑙 𝑗 for each 𝑗 ∈ [1, 𝑚]. Then, 𝑢 𝑗 = 𝑙 𝑗 + 𝜆× domain size, where 𝜆 ∈ [0.2, 0.8]. By default, 𝜆 = 0.2 and 𝑘 = 10. In this default setting, the average selectivity (i.e., the ratio of the objects satisfying the range filter) was 0.15. Evaluated algorithms. For algorithms that do not require past query workloads, we evaluated the following ones: • BF: A brute-force exact algorithm. • Pre-filter: This algorithm employs a kd-tree based on the attribute values of the objects in 𝑋. Given a query, it first traverses the kd-tree based on the query range filters and obtains a set of objects that satisfy the range filters. Then, it runs a linear scan of this set to return the 𝑘NN vectors, so this algorithm also returns the exact answer. This algorithm actually corresponds Milvus [46]. Navix [41] also follows this approach but returns an approximate result. We tested Navix, but its performance was worse than the exact version of Pre-filter, so we omit its result. • IVF: An ANNS algorithm that is based on an inverted file structure. This approach is widely employed in the state-of- the-art ANNS systems [46, 50, 34]. • Post-filter: The baseline algorithm introduced in Section 2. We used HNSW [33] as its ANNS index. This algorithm actually corresponds to SIEVE [29] without past query filters (see Section 3) and VBase [57]. • ACORN: The baseline algorithm introduced in Section 2. Because ACORN-𝛾 [37] could not be built in a reasonable time (i.e., 1 hour), we used ACORN-1. • Grant-basic: Our algorithm described in Section 4.2. We used a kd-tree as the base tree structure, and each leaf node maintains the corresponding objects by HNSW. This setting was applied to the next algorithms. We set 𝑐 = 150 (see our supplementary). • Grant-pnv: Our algorithm with the probabilistic node verification heuristic. For algorithms that require past query workloads, we evaluated • WA-Grant: Our algorithm that exploits past query vectors, see Section 4.4. For each dataset, we randomly sampled 1,000 vectors and added Gaussian noise to them. We used them as past query vectors, and they were also indexed by an HNSW. 8

All algorithms were implemented in C++ and compiled by g++ 11.3.0 with -O3 optimization. They enabled SIMD instruc- tions. For the algorithms using HNSW, we used the original implementation 4 . We tuned the inner parameters to obtain a Pareto-optimal QPS-recall tradeoff. For HNSW, we did a grid search from 𝑀 = {8, 16, 32, 64, 128} and 𝑒𝑓 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 = {32, 64, 100, 200, 300}. As a result, we set 𝑀 = 64 and 𝑒𝑓 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 = 200 for the baselines, whereas we set 𝑀 = 16 and 𝑒𝑓 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 = 64 for Grant. (Since each leaf node has at most 𝑛/𝑐 < 𝑛 vectors, each HNSW in Grant has smaller parameter values.) For IVF, we used 1,000 clusters. We did not consider works that assume matching filters on multiple attributes [20, 48], as they are not trivial to efficiently address our problem. A straightforward extension of matching filter techniques to range filters requires discretizing each continuous range into a very large number of (in principle, infinitely many) equality predicates, which is impractical. 5.2 Result We first report the performances of the algorithms that do not require past query workloads. For indexing time, memory usage, impact of 𝑐, impact of 𝑘, impact of 𝑚, and impact of range size, refer to our supplementary. Impact of 𝑐. We tuned 𝑐 for Grant, and Figure 3 shows QPS (queries per second) under recall ≈ 0.9 on SIFT and SPACEV. Note that (i) we have similar results on Deep and T2I and (ii) the “< 76” case shows the best result when 𝑐 ≤ 75. Although Grant is not very sensitive to 𝑐, it has an optimal 𝑐. When 𝑐 is large, we have many leaf nodes overlapping 𝐹 , so it incurs many ANNSs. On the other hand, when 𝑐 is small, we have fewer leaf nodes overlapping 𝐹 but have a larger number of objects that do not satisfy 𝐹 . These observations yield the results in Figure 3. Indexing time. Table 2 shows the indexing time of each algorithm. (Since BF does not employ any data structure, it is omitted.) This phase used 24 threads. Grant-basic and Grant-pnv share the same data structure, so their indexing time is represented by Grant. Since Pre-filter employs a single tree structure based only on attributes, it needs a shorter indexing time than the others. Although Grant employs tree and graph structures, its indexing time is at most just 1.5 minutes for 10 million high- dimensional vectors. An interesting observation is that Grant needs shorter indexing time than IVF, Post-filter, and ACORN. Memory consumption. Table 3 exhibits the memory consumption of the data structure of each algorithm. Because of the graph-based indices, Post-filter and our algorithm needs more memory than Pre-filter and IVF. Nonetheless, our algorithm does not consume much memory, and only less than about 10GB is required for 10 million high-dimensional vectors, which is easy to fit into modern servers. (ACORN employs a graph index that is essentially HNSW, so its memory consumption is almost the same as Post-filter.) QPS vs. recall. We compare our algorithms with the baseline ones w.r.t. time and accuracy tradeoff. Figure 4 plots the QPS vs. recall curve of each algorithm. (This observation can be seen by comparing the results in Figures 4 and 5.) 6 Conclusion This paper addressed the problem of ANNS with multi-attribute range filters and proposed Grant, a new data structure that solves this problem efficiently. Our theoretical analysis proves the efficiency of Grant. In addition, we proposed two heuristics that optimized the query processing performance of Grant. Our experiments demonstrate that Grant outperforms the existing state-of-the-art techniques. Limitation. This work considers a static dataset, and how to efficiently deal with dynamic data (i.e., vector insertions and deletions) is an open problem. In addition, this work assumes that 𝑚 is small because real-world datasets have this tendency (e.g., price, rating, and date), and it is highly unlikely that ranges are specified for many attributes. If this assumption does not hold, the Grant structure may not be efficient because the tree structure is efficient only when 𝑚 (or dimensionality) is small (although, due to the curse of dimensionality, it is common to degrade the performance of a given algorithm for large 𝑚). Figure 6 illustrates the result under recall ≈ 0.9. We omit Grant-basic because Grant-pnv is always better. The QPS of Grant-pnv decreases as 𝑘 increases. Nevertheless, it is much better than the existing algorithms. BF, Pre-filter, and IVF are not affected by 𝑘 because they access all objects in 𝑋, all objects in a result set of the range search, and all objects in the corresponding posting lists, respectively. As 𝑘 becomes larger, the QPS of Post-filter becomes very low (e.g., less than 40 for 𝑘 = 50) because Post-filter needs to iterate more ANNS. ACORN failed to obtain nearly 0.9 recall (so it does not have plots) when 𝑘 ≥ 20, because its graph traversal approach loses the path to reach the exact 𝑘NN objects. Impact of 𝑚. We next study the impact of the number of attributes 𝑚. Figure 7 shows that our algorithm keeps outper- forming the other ones. Recall the time complexity of our algorithm, and its empirical performance follows the theoretical result. We see that Post-filter and Pre-filter have the opposite tendency. Post-filter is very sensitive to 𝑚, whereas Pre-filter improves its efficiency with a larger 𝑚. This is because a larger 𝑚 usually yields a smaller range search result set. ACORN again failed to obtain nearly 0.9 recall when 𝑚 ≥ 3. These results demonstrate that ACORN is not appropriate for our problem. Impact of range size. To investigate the impact of range size (i.e., |𝑋(𝐹 )|), we ran experiments by varying 𝜆. Figure 8 exhibits the robustness of our algorithm against range size. This robustness is attributed to their unnecessary leaf node skipping heuristics. A larger range size provides a larger 𝑋(𝐹 ), so the performance of Pre-filter (Post-filter) becomes lower (higher) as 𝜆 becomes larger. The performance of Post-filter did not reach that of our algorithm even when 𝜆 is large. 11
